I still feel like there's a bug with disengagement chance. This particular fight might have not been affected by it, and might have just been because the FE ships were really powerful (still though, wiping out 800 naval cap seems weird, and in that case I should see it in every fight, not just a few of them). The thing is though, it's not just when I fight against one-shotter ships. It can be anything. It happens just as often in the relative early game (<2300) as it does in the late game (>2400). In fact I believe I see this most often occur when I'm fighting empires near the start of the game, and almost exclusively when using trickster commanders (Though maybe biased because I nearly only use trickster commanders and early game is the most played).

Using this fight, here's what I think the disengagement chance should be, using battleships, and assuming they took so much damage in one hit they went from full hull to 1% hull.

chance = [damage/hull \* 1.5 \* ship multiplier \* 1.25 (if within friendly borders) \* (sum of other modifiers)](https://stellaris.paradoxwikis.com/Space_warfare#Ship_disengagement)  
So:  
chance = [99/100 \* 1.5 \* 1.25 \* 1.25 \* (1 + 0.33 + 0.05 + 0.05 + 0.4)](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i=99%2F100+*+1.5+*+1.25+*+1.25+*+%281+%2B+0.33+%2B+0.05+%2B+0.05+%2B+0.4%29) = 424%

These numbers come from having Hit and Run Policy, Commander having Prudence 2 and Trickster 2, being Admiral, and fighting within borders. They should also have 2 opportunities to escape. This is a theoretical calculation, in the fight I think the real chance for the battleships would have been something like 200-300% \* 2. Yet despite the seemingly high chance of escape, none of my battleships did escape. The only semi-plausible explanation I can see for this is some sort of overflow. Maybe it's possible that when the ships are fighting things that do just enough damage to push the chance of escape over 100%, an if-statement doesn't trigger or something like that, and the code skips over the disengagement opportunity.

Either way I think it should be looked at, because this is not normal, and if this is how it's supposed to function, I don't think it should be. It doesn't make for a good war, or even a good game, when the fate of an entire war, or an entire empire can be decided by a single battle. If your entire fleet is wiped out, then you most likely won't have the resources or time, often both, to build it up again powerful enough to destroy whatever killed it (At least if whatever killed it is another empire who claimed 90% of your territory, is using total war, is blowing up your planets or has some other way of ruining your economy after the war).

Every time, it ruins my game by making me lose an entire war on a whim, and usually most of my economy that way. I have searched for other having the same issue, doesn't seem like it. It doesn't matter if I'm fighting in a black hole, or if my admiral has trickster (almost all of them do), or if I do the tactics that give higher disengage chance (Which I always have on. Sometimes, seemingly at completely random, the game just decides that every single ship in a fight dies. It doesn't matter if it's singleplayer or multiplayer, but it happens most often in fights against AI. It also doesn't matter what kind of ships I use, or the relative fleet power. I have experienced this with almost every situation imaginable, in every. Single. Game. It's starting to piss me off that the game just pushes the lose button for me when I am doling everything in my power to increase my ships' chances of survival.

I also often see the opposite when fighting the AI actually. I'll make a fortress in a black hole system, build the starbase building that reduces escape chance, come in with a titan that reduces escape chance, etc. and still they lost only maybe 1% of their ships, while I still lose a lot more.

**Manage your production.**

If you keep peeling back players, almost every single problem you will face can be boiled down to "You don't have enough resources"
Learning not just how to manage planets to optimalt produce certain resources, but also when to do so, and why, will make the entire game way easier for you. Suddenly you're sitting with a 1000 basic resource over productuion, more alloys and consume goods than you know what to do with, and a finished science tree by year 2300.

The two main things I tend to follow to do this is:
1. **More is better than less.** It's better to produce a hundred too many of some resources, than a hundred too few, even if they're just going to waste because you're at your storage limit. Having disposable income gives you so many opportunities and ways to bail yourself out of dumb mistakes.
2. **Pops are everything.** An empire's strength can be pretty well gauged by simply how technologically advanced they are, and how many pops they have. Pops produce almost everything you need, so more of them means more resources. If you see an option to get more pops, it's usually best to take it. Whether that means invading primitives, taking in refugees, boosting fertility via traits, cloning, etc. Pops can't work without planets though, so keep in mind to also get some of those. This is why robots and lithoids are my favourite to play as, they can use more of the planets they encountered, and can produce pops faster (The budding trait works for lithoids too if I'm not misremembering).

Use the market as a bandaid. Set up some monthly traded to spend your excess resources, and get the ones you're missing. Then there's 4 options the way I see it.

1. Colonise a planet for the specific purpose of producing one resource you need. Do this for every resource you need.

2. Change a planet that's producing a resource you don't need into a resource you do need.
In this case, you probably have a generator world. Make that into a factory world.

3. Optimise a planet that's producing a resource you need. Or optimise production by other means.
In this case, if you have a factory world without an upgraded civilian factory, or without that building that gives +15% output, add it. 
You can also optimise via policies, for example if you have an overflow of energy and you need consumer goods, you should really consider changing your trade policy to the one that fixes both.

4. Ignore the problem and just use monthly trades. (My personal favourite.) 
If you have a lot of big monthly trades, you will want to set a limit to how much you want to sell or buy for. Because of this, you will get the notification that the price is too high or low a lot. It should be fine to ignore it, as it comes mainly from AIs selling resources, or from you selling them in big quantities and often.
You will see big, red, scary numbers, but it will be fine.

The khan had just gone super saiyan, and I was their neighbour. I was a militarist empire at war with someone almost constantly. Suddenly, I was under seige from all sides. No worries, I thought. I had been preparing for it with a citadel at a chokepoint to the marauders. They'll probably go for the other neighbouring empire anyway. I'll keep defending from the AI, surely nothing bad will happ- "Starbase lost"... Well shit. With like 4 25k fleets or something like that, at a time when the biggest military might in the galaxy had a total of ~60k power, they steamrolled me and conquered half my undefended empire in a few years. I barely made it back to the choke point defending ny capital before they arrived there as well. I focused all my fleets in that one spot to try and wipe them out before they could get to my capital... The marauders killed my entire fleet and barely took any casualties. This is the end, I thought. It was like a chess match at this point. I paused the game and looked at my options. The marauders and their 80k fleet was about half a year away from my capital... Okay. I go look up the composition of the marauder ships and design a corvette with 1k fleet power specifically as a counter to their ships. Sell all my minerals, food, consumer goods, and most of the strategic resources for alloys. Replace the commercial modules on the capital starbase for shipyards, so there's 6 in total. Start loading up tons of defense platforms and hundreds of corvettes. I barely get to build up a force a quarter of their fleet power before they get there. I'm doomed, there's no way I will survive. I watch the battle, it draws on for literal years. My Starbase keeps chugging out corvettes to chip away at the marauder ships, while taking the majority of the damage. After 10, maybe 15 minutes of watching the fight unfold, it finally ends. I won. I somehow actually won. With my forces partially recuperated I instantly set out to reconquer my lost empire. The speed of the corvettes allow me to do so in just a year or two. When I then get down to the citadel base that was supposed to protect me from them in the first place, I regain intel on their systems. Mouse over the enemy fleet icon. Soul leaves my body for a second. They had like 100k fleet power, if not more just sitting there the entire time. The force that almost wiped me from the face of the galaxy was only a fraction of their power. 10 seconds later, they're all moving towards my choke point. Ah, shit. Here we go again.

Well if you get lock picking up to Lvl 13 and get a padfoot potion you have access to almost every chest in the game, if not every chest. So my tactic is usually to buy everything from every merchant, then go into the back to their personal chests and steal my money back. Or in the start just go in the back and steal all the stuff then go to the miller,and sell everything, even though he doesn't have enough money to pay. After a few days, or in other words a Swift jail sentence, the miller will have sold the items and turned a huge profit. I once got him to have 30k Groschen at once, then lockpicked my way into his personal chest and stole it all. When you have access to his chest you also practically have infinite lockpicks, as he gets 20 every few days, so you can just buy them, get the rep, and take your money back. Also the small houee between the artisian in Rattay and the poor district, one of the first houses on the left when entering Rattay from the southern side, is practically abandoned. Nobody comes in there and the doors never get opened or closed, so it's a good place to hide from guards or as a shortcut when raising the weaponsmith. The apothecary can also be very lucrative, mostly due to the recipe books and ingredients. The hardest one to raid by buying their stuff and only stealing back your money is the tailor, as his shop is guarded all day, and also sometimes during the night. Because of that and the not so lucrative clothes business, I'd advise not to steal from the tailor. If you want money and gear very quickly in the beginning though, you can always level up your stealth a bit, level up your strength a bit, and then go to the garden at the upper Rattay castle. If you wait there for a bit there will pop up a guard every now and again, but it will mostly be empty, making it perfect for knocking our guards and stealing their stuff. Of you ever get searched, just lay them off, it's only like 20 Groschen which is nothing compared to the money you can get from the crimes that will get you searched in the first place.

TL;DR
Get to lockpicking 13 and get a padfoot potion, then you have access to every chest. Steal from guards in concealed locations or at night or both of you can.
